newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong candidate says would legalise communists.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong candidate says would legalise communists.

text.p: The man tipped as the favourite to become Hong Kong's future leader, tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, said on Tuesday he would legalise the Communist Party after the British colony reverts to China next year.
"Certainly yes," Tung told a reporter when asked if he would legalise the party.

The billionaire shipping magnate, who finished first in the initial round of balloting for Hong Kong's next chief executive, had just finished a speech to a business group where he painted a rosy picture of Hong Kong's future under Chinese rule.

Although China is ruled by the Communist Party, Beijing has pledged to grant Hong Kong great autonomy and to leave its capitalist system intact for 50 years under the policy of "Hong Kong people running Hong Kong" and "one country two systems".
All political parties were outlawed in Hong Kong by the colonial authorities until reforms in 1990. The status of the Chinese Communist Party remains a grey area.
In the past the party was involved in violent conflicts with the colonial government, especially during the bloody Hong Kong riots of 1967 inspired by China's radical left-wing Cultural Revolution.
Hong Kong Security Branch spokesman Mak Kwok-wah told Reuters the Communist Party was not legally registered at present in Hong Kong.
"There is no such entity in Hong Kong," he said. But most officials and politicians agree there are communists in Hong Kong but they do not declare themselves as such.
Tung said he hoped communists would be tolerated in Hong Kong in future.
"I think there are Communist Party members in Hong Kong now. Indeed they will continue to be here. I do not know what their own plans are, whether they want to be legalised or not.

"But I would imagine that Hong Kong is a very tolerant society, and that political activity of different kinds will be acceptable here so long as it is in the broader framework of stability and making things here better."

Tung is widely tipped to be Beijing's choice for chief executive after the handover, and last week captured 51 percent of the votes from the 400-member Selection Committee created under China's supervision that is choosing the future leader.
The result left Tung facing only two other contenders. The committee will cast its final vote on December 11 and Tung is expected to win.
Hong Kong reverts to China next July under a 1984 treaty. The territory was ceded to Britain by imperial China after the "opium war" a century and a half ago.
Tung was also asked what would be the role of China's de facto embassy in the territory, the Xinhua News Agency office, after the 1997 handover. He said it was up to Beijing.

"The role of Xinhua will be a decision for the central government. But any decision made by the central authorities will not undermine the principle of 'Hong Kong people running Hong Kong' and 'One Country, Two Systems'.
"There will be no overlord," he said.

In his speech to the World Economic Forum meeting, Tung painted an optimistic picture of Hong Kong's outlook under Chinese rule and said it was time to focus less on politics and more on economics to ensure the bustling capitalist outpost remained highly competitive.
In recent years most Hong Kong people have been intensely watching developments linked to the 1997 handover.
